description: Low-power pose holding for the Aero Hand (software). The servos have no brake, so holding a pose against the return springs, an object or a hand costs current and heat (2026-10-17: about 2000-2400 current units on thumb flex, ring and pinky while Jake held the hand; ring and pinky climbed past 63-65 C). After a pose is reached, drop each servo's torque (SET_TOR) to the lowest value that still holds it against its spring, with a small margin, and raise it again for the next move. Detect stalls (high current with little motion) and back off. MEASURE first: write a repeatable benchmark (e.g. hold fist, peace and the can grip in free air for 60 s each, logging per-servo current and temperature rise per minute, starting from a similar temperature). Record the baseline BEFORE changing anything, then the same numbers after, and put both in the README with the improvement. Applies to pose.py, grip.py, and the Mac app's buttons. Keep the 50% speed default.

results.identified_issue: Holding current was mostly stall current. In position mode the Feetech HLS servos pin current at the WritePosEx torque limit (~3-6.5 mA per unit) when short of target. Commanding the settled actuations (hand.set_actuations(ref)) removes that error, and the SET_TOR step-down then finds the spring+friction floor. Firmware only applies SET_TOR on the next CTRL_POS, and g_torque persists in firmware RAM across scripts, hence engage(700) before every move. Probe 2026-10-17 (fist, held at settled pos, 1 s per level): fingers held at 35 and sagged at 25; thumb flex sagged at 75; thumb abd/tendon held at 8. Margin 1.5 is unverified for long holds or when the hand is bumped. A sagged servo isn't re-raised later because the script exits after the hold. Not applied to performance.py, teleop.py or rps.py (continuous motion). The grip stall back-off (start//2) is untested with an object. The baseline assumed torque 700 everywhere; pose.py previously inherited whatever torque was last set (grip.py leaves 300 or 1000).
results.summary: Poses now hold on about a quarter of the power: fist 12.1 A → 3.1 A total, peace 8.9 → 2.2 A, can grip 5.9 → 1.8 A, and ring/pinky stopped heating (was +13 °C/min).
results.detailed_description:
I measured first, then changed the code. hold_bench.py relaxes the hand, waits until every servo is at 50 °C or below, runs the real command (pose.py fist, pose.py peace, grip.py close for the can grip), and logs current and temperature for 60 s in free air. Baseline (move torque 700, the firmware default): fist 12124 mA total, peace 8877, can 5938. Ring and pinky climbed +12-14 °C/min, reaching 61-64 °C in one minute. The curled fingers were each drawing ~2000 mA, right at their torque limit: they stop just short of 90° (on the palm or their end stop) and keep pushing forever.

The fix (scripts/hold.py, called by pose.py and grip.py, so the app's pose buttons get it too): once a pose is reached, each servo is told to hold where it actually settled instead of the unreachable target. Then its torque limit steps down from 450 to 10 until it sags more than 2°, and it keeps 1.5x the lowest level that held. Every new move first raises all servos back to 700. After: fist 3068 mA (-75%), peace 2212 (-75%), can 1798 (-70%), and ring/pinky rose 0 °C over the minute. Both tables are in third_party/aero_hand/README.md, with raw data in bench/.

Things to know: the step-down adds about 4 s of small, barely visible adjustment after each pose. The torque steps, the 2° sag limit and the 1.5x margin are hardcoded constants at the top of hold.py. Count-to-ten only does it on the last number. In grip.py a finger stalled on an object keeps half the grip torque (150) so it doesn't let go. I haven't tried that with a real can, so test it, and use grip.py --torque if it slips. Thumb flex is now the biggest draw (~960 mA; it sags below ~100), so it's the next one to look at. Speed stays 50%.

Heat safety, per your note: the benchmark relaxes everything and aborts a pose the moment any servo reads 68 °C (2 °C under your 70, because the sensor reads whole degrees), and it never starts a pose above 54 °C. The highest it logged was 64 °C (baseline fist/peace pinky). The 72-75 °C you saw didn't come from a benchmark run, so something else must have been driving the hand then.
results.user_reply_draft: Done. The hand now holds poses on about a quarter of the power. I measured first: holding a fist drew about 12 amps total and ring and pinky heated about 13 °C per minute. With the fix it's about 3 amps and they stay flat. Peace and the can grip improved the same way. The trick is letting each finger hold where it actually stopped instead of pushing into the palm, then turning its strength down to just what it needs. Try a fist from the app and feel how cool it stays; and if a real can slips out of the grip, tell me.

summary: Aero Hand servos have no brake, so holding poses against springs or objects draws high current and overheats them. Lower each servo's torque once a pose is reached, backing off on stalls, and prove it with before-and-after benchmarks in the README.
